name: Haskalah
info: The Haskalah, often called the Jewish Enlightenment, was an intellectual movement among the Jews of Central and Eastern Europe from the 1770s to the close of the 19th century, which pressed for Hebrew revival, secular education and integration.

facts.where: Central and Eastern Europe, beginning in Berlin; later Vienna, Prague, Galicia, Vilnius, Warsaw and Odessa, the Pale of Settlement and Congress Poland; a certain influence in Western Europe and the Muslim world
facts.period: arose as a defined worldview in the 1770s in Berlin; spread through Europe in the 19th century; its last stage ended at the close of the 19th century, after the 1881 pogroms in Imperial Russia
facts.figures: Moses Mendelssohn, philosopher and translator of the Torah into German; Naphtali Hirz Wessely, poet and author of Words of Peace and Truth; Isaac Euchel, founder of Ha-Meassef; Joseph Perl, satirist and school founder; Isaac Baer Levinsohn, called the Russian Mendelssohn; Abraham Mapu, novelist; Judah Leib Gordon, poet; Aleksander Zederbaum, editor of Ha-Melitz
facts.outcome: it revived Hebrew as a literary language and helped modernise education and culture among Central and Eastern European Jews, but its later historians judge its part limited; its adherents were divided, and after the 1881 pogroms many turned towards proto-Zionist groups

t: The maskilim, as the movement's activists were called, sought to revive Hebrew as a language of secular literature, teach general subjects alongside Jewish ones, and bring Jews into the surrounding societies without ending Jewish distinctness.

The movement clashed with the traditionalist rabbinic elite, which wished to keep old Jewish values and norms in full, and also with radical assimilationists, whom the maskilim called pseudo-maskilim.

Historians once treated the Haskalah as the main cause of the changes in Jewish society, but later research narrowed its importance: state schools and new economic opportunities rivalled or overshadowed it, and in many regions it had no effect at all.
dyk: Abraham Mapu's Ahavat Zion, the first full-length Hebrew novel, was published in 1853 after twenty-three years of work.
ev: Moses Mendelssohn begins publishing Qohelet Musar, regarded as the first journal in Hebrew and the beginning of modern writing in the language
Maskilim help to found the Berlin Jewish Free School, the first institution among Ashkenazi Jews to teach general studies beside a reduced traditional curriculum
Hartwig Wessely circulates Divrei Shalom v'Emeth, calling on Jews to add science and the vernacular language to their children's curriculum
Isaac Abraham Euchel launches the quarterly Ha-Meassef in Königsberg, whose publishers call themselves Maskilim
Joseph Perl opens the first modern Jewish school in Galicia at Tarnopol
Joseph Perl publishes Megaleh Tmirin, a satire on Hasidic Judaism
Aleksander Zederbaum launches Ha-Melitz in Odessa, whose motto makes Haskalah the standard name of the movement
Pogroms in Imperial Russia lead many adherents of the Haskalah to turn towards proto-Zionist groups such as Hibbat Zion

sections.background:
As long as Jews lived in segregated communities and contact with their gentile neighbours was limited, the rabbi was the most influential member of the Jewish community. Besides being a religious scholar, a rabbi acted as a civil judge in all cases in which both parties were Jews, and sometimes held other administrative powers together with the community elders. The rabbinate was the highest aim of many Jewish boys, and study of the Talmud was the way to it. The rabbinic courts and the board of elders were the traditional community institutions that the maskilim later sought to limit.

The example of Moses Mendelssohn (1729–86), a Prussian Jew, led the movement. His success as a philosopher and man of letters revealed possibilities of integration and acceptance of Jews among non-Jews. Knowledge of German was necessary to enter cultured German circles, and Mendelssohn provided a means of acquiring it in his German translation of the Torah, which became a bridge for ambitious young Jews into the world of secular knowledge. The Biur, a grammatical commentary prepared under his supervision, was designed to counteract traditional rabbinical methods of exegesis.

Berlin was the city of origin. Its middle-class Jews and intellectual elites were exposed to Enlightenment thinkers such as Voltaire, Diderot and Rousseau, and the movement is often called the Berlin Haskalah. A further precondition was a cultural change among the Parnassim, the affluent communal wardens, who were open to outside society and had to teach their children secular subjects.
sections.aims:
The Haskalah arose as a defined ideological worldview in the 1770s, as its proponents engaged with the philosophical and scientific ideas of the Age of Enlightenment. The maskilim wished to replace the values of the Ashkenazim of Central and Eastern Europe with a philosophy that embraced the liberal, rationalistic notions of the 18th and 19th centuries. Even the moderates thought the state of the Jews deplorable in morals, cultural creativity and economic productivity, and held that the base and corrupt elements of Jewish existence should be shed and only the true, positive ones kept.

Their programme was practical. They urged Jews to learn European culture and the language of their lands, to discard traditional dress, and to be patriotic and loyal to the new centralised governments. They opposed self-segregation and criticised child marriage, the use of anathema to enforce community will, and the concentration on almost only religious studies. They preached agriculture, trades and the liberal professions in place of traditional Jewish occupations.

Language stood at the centre. The maskilim wanted a refined Hebrew for internal use and the local vernacular for external dealings, and they almost universally abhorred Yiddish, then called Judaeo-German, as a corrupt dialect. On faith they had no uniform agenda: they judged Judaism by rationalism, revived Jewish philosophy as an alternative to Kabbalah, and sought a literal reading of scripture. Some on the right only wanted a rationalist approach; on the extreme left some ventured towards Deism.
sections.events:
The literary beginnings came first. In 1755 Mendelssohn began publishing Qohelet Musar, the first journal in Hebrew. In 1778 supporters of the movement were among the founders of the Berlin Jewish Free School, which taught general studies in addition to a reformulated and reduced traditional curriculum. In 1782 Hartwig Wessely, one of the most traditional and moderate maskilim, circulated Divrei Shalom v'Emeth, urging that science and the vernacular enter the curriculum. Historian Shmuel Feiner judged that Wessely, consciously or not, insinuated a challenge to the supremacy of sacred teachings, which mobilised the rabbis against the nascent Haskalah.

In 1783 Isaac Abraham Euchel launched Ha-Meassef in Königsberg, later Berlin; at its height it had 272 subscribers from Shklow in the east to London in the west, and it was printed with growing intervals until 1797. Later periodicals included Bikurei ha-I'tim in Vienna (1820–1831), Kerem Hemed in Prague (1834–1857), Ha-Karmel in Vilnius (1860–1880), Ha-Tsefirah in Warsaw and Ha-Melitz in Odessa, launched in 1860.

The movement spread to Eastern Europe, where Joseph Perl opened the first modern Jewish school in Galicia at Tarnopol in 1813 and published his satire on Hasidic Judaism, Megaleh Tmirin, in 1819. Maskilim there worked with the Russian government of the Pale of Settlement on secular education. The pogroms of 1881 in Imperial Russia ended its last stage, as many adherents turned towards proto-Zionist groups like Hibbat Zion.
sections.people:
Moses Mendelssohn, philosopher and man of letters, was a central founder; his students started Ha-Meassef, and the Berlin circle also included Naphtali Hirz Wessely, Isaac Satanow and Isaac Euchel, whose tracts formed the first shared literary canon. Wessely compiled the eighteen-part epic cycle Shirei Tif'eret about Moses from 1789. Aaron Halle-Wolfssohn wrote the first modern Judaeo-German play, Leichtsinn und Frömmelei, in 1796. Joseph ha-Efrati Troplowitz, the pioneering playwright, wrote Melukhat Sha'ul in 1794, and Judah Leib Ben-Ze'ev, the first modern Hebrew grammarian, published a manual of the language in 1796.

In the east, Joseph Perl pioneered satire in Megaleh Tmirin. Isaac Baer Levinsohn became known as the Russian Mendelssohn. Avraham Dov Ber Lebensohn, a leading metricist, published Shirei S'fat haQodesh in 1842. Abraham Mapu wrote Ahavat Zion, the first Hebrew full-length novel, in 1853. Judah Leib Gordon was the most eminent poet of his generation and arguably of the whole Haskalah; his best-known work was the 1876 epic Qotzo shel Yodh. Solomon Löwisohn was the first to translate Shakespeare into Hebrew. Aleksander Zederbaum edited Ha-Melitz.

Nearly all maskilim had an old-style secluded education and were young Torah scholars before meeting outside knowledge. The movement was almost totally male-dominated, as women did not receive enough tutoring to master Hebrew. Most maskilim lived by private tutoring and similar work, and needed patrons, either affluent Jews or state institutions.
sections.outcomes:
The Haskalah produced the first phase of modern Hebrew literature and carried out communal, educational and cultural reforms, but it was a limited part of the modernisation of Central and Eastern European Jews. It was weak and dependent on far stronger elements. The government wanted only productive, loyal subjects with rudimentary secular education, and had no interest in the maskilim's visions of renaissance. Rich Jews were mostly practical, hoping for a betterment that would bring emancipation and equal rights. Frustration with apathetic Jews, whether conservative fanatics or parvenu assimilationists, is a common theme in the movement's literature.

It was marked by a dual agenda. The maskilim urged Jews to acculturate to the modern state and also to remain a distinct group with its own culture. They drew a line between themselves and the pseudo-maskilim who sought full assimilation, and some were not fully agreeable to civic emancipation. The movement was largely unigenerational: the children of maskilim almost never followed their parents, and often lacked Hebrew. In Central Europe acculturation far exceeded the movement's plans, and the journal Sulamith, begun in 1806, was written almost entirely in German.

Later research narrowed the movement's importance. Historians such as Heinrich Graetz had depicted it as a major factor in the changes of Jewish society, but the contemporary historical consensus portrays it as much humbler. State schools and new economic opportunities rivalled or overshadowed it, and in many regions it had no effect at all.
sections.legacy:
The Haskalah led to a secular Jewish culture with an emphasis on Jewish history and identity rather than religion, and to political engagement over emancipation, new Jewish political movements and later, in the face of continued persecutions, Zionism. One commentator described emancipation as producing two opposed movements: cultural assimilation, begun by Moses Mendelssohn, and Zionism, founded by Theodor Herzl in 1896.

It also shaped religious life. The Reform movement was born with founders such as Israel Jacobson and Leopold Zunz, who rejected the observance of aspects of Jewish law they classed as ritual rather than moral. Groups such as the Society of the Friends of Reform and the Association for the Reform of Judaism wanted change, for example regarding circumcision. Within Orthodoxy the Mussar Movement in Lithuania and Torah im Derech Eretz in Germany appeared in response. Orthodox Jews opposed the reformers, who in their view insulted God by changing tradition.

Later movements judged the Haskalah harshly. The Jewish national movements of Eastern Europe, founded by disillusioned maskilim, regarded it as a naive, liberal and assimilationist ideology that promised false hopes of equality; nationalist thinkers and historians such as Peretz Smolenskin, Ahad Ha'am and Simon Dubnow held this view, once common in Israeli historiography. Mendele Mocher Sforim's Beseter ra'am of 1886 is taken to mark the end of the Maskilic period in Hebrew literature and the beginning of the Era of Renaissance.

summary: The Haskalah, or Jewish Enlightenment, was a movement among Central and Eastern European Jews from the 1770s to the end of the 19th century. Its maskilim revived Hebrew as a secular literary language and urged education and integration, clashing with rabbinic traditionalists and with assimilationists. Later historians judge its effect limited.
notes: Dates: the article says the movement arose as a defined worldview during the 1770s and that its last stage ended at the close of the 19th century (the 1881 pogroms are the stated turning point). I set start 1770 and end 1900, both approximate. The article also dates Mendelssohn's Qohelet Musar to 1755, treated as the beginning of modern Hebrew writing, which is listed as an event.
The article dates the name Haskalah as a standard self-appellation to 1860 (Ha-Melitz); Maskil was common by 1783 in Ha-Meassef.
Mendelssohn's lifespan is given 1729–86 in Origins and 1729-1786 in the list. Halle-Wolfssohn is 1754–1835 in one place and 1754/6 to 1835 in another; I used no birth year.

Megaleh Tmirin: the article says it is said to be the first modern novel in Hebrew (Spread section), while the Literary circle section says Mapu authored the first Hebrew full-length novel (1853). I give Mapu's claim as stated and describe Perl's work only as a satire.
Ha-Meassef: first said to be launched by Euchel in 1783 and 'students of Mendelssohn' in the Definitions section; I used both as stated. Spelling Ha-Meassef/Ha-Meassif varies; I used Ha-Meassef.
Left out: the list of Maskilim (little detail), Mendelssohn's views on Jesus and Islam, Julius Fürst, the Conservative Jews' origin, and the Mussar movement detail beyond a mention.
'Judaeo-German' is the article's term for Yiddish; the article also says Yiddish elsewhere.
